routes.description: Establish reflective Christianity as credible through a cumulative case from philosophical reasoning, scriptural and experiential considerations, and resurrection evidence, while limiting skeptical inferences from evil, disagreement, expert dissent, and Christian moral failure.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the positive considerations provide reasonable warrant for Christianity and the negative considerations neither render its core claims unlikely nor defeat the cumulative case when assessed together.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative positive case and the answers to skeptical objections to the conclusion that reflective Christianity remains credible.

centralBridges.description: Show that philosophical arguments can provide discriminating support for theism despite uncertainty about premises, divine motivations, and evidential partitioning.
Show that revelation, religious experience, and resurrection considerations supply warrant for distinctively Christian claims rather than generic theism alone.
Show that evil, religious disagreement, expert dissent, and moral failure do not outweigh or defeat the positive cumulative case.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Specify when cognitive limits and consequential complexity legitimately restrict skeptical likelihood judgments without indiscriminately defeating positive arguments.
Distinguish reasonable Christian credibility from certainty and explain why acknowledged disagreement need not require an atheistic conclusion.

routes.description: Establish skeptical atheism by challenging the predictive and explanatory force of the positive Christian considerations and presenting evil, religious disagreement, expert dissent, and Christian moral failure as cumulative evidence against Christianity.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the positive arguments fail to make Christianity sufficiently probable and the negative considerations are better expected without the Christian account of God, revelation, resurrection, and transformation.

motionBridge.description: Connect the failure of the positive case and the cumulative skeptical evidence to the conclusion that Christianity is unlikely.

centralBridges.description: Show that philosophical arguments, biblical beauty, religious experience, and resurrection evidence lack the claimed discriminatory or explanatory force.
Show that apparently preventable suffering and persistent religious confusion are less expected under the proposed Christian God than under naturalism.
Show that informed dissent and the observed moral record materially reduce confidence in Christianity's truth and transformative claims.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Supply naturalistic explanations for fine-tuning and resurrection data that avoid disputed assumptions about divine psychology or miraculous intervention.
Require consistent treatment of uncertainty, cognitive limitation, comparative expertise, and likelihood reasoning across positive and negative arguments.

sections.title: Philosophical Arguments, Fine-Tuning, and Divine Psychology
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether philosophical and fine-tuning arguments predict a life-permitting universe under theism or instead depend on uncertain premises, contested value theories, and arbitrary evidential partitions.

sections.title: Scripture, Religious Experience, and Reflective Warrant
sections.rationale: This issue concerns whether biblical qualities and religious experience distinguish Christian revelation and justify reflective belief despite rival experiences, counterarguments, and disagreement.

sections.title: Resurrection Evidence and Naturalistic Explanation
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether physical resurrection best explains the burial, appearances, and resulting bodily-resurrection belief or whether a naturalistic sequence explains the same evidence.

sections.title: Evil, Religious Disagreement, and Epistemic Limitation
sections.rationale: This issue bears directly on whether suffering and failed or uneven revelation are improbable under Christianity, and whether appeals to consequential complexity or cognitive limits answer those inferences consistently.

sections.title: Expert Dissent, Rational Confidence, and Christian Moral Fruit
sections.rationale: This issue examines how interdisciplinary and specialist disagreement should constrain confidence and whether Christianity's claimed moral transformation generates unmet observable expectations relevant to credibility.

moves.speaker: James Fodor
moves.proposition: Philosophical arguments for God depend on numerous uncertain assumptions and speculative inferences about divine desires, motivations, and reasons for acting.
moves.attributionBasis: The host explicitly solicits Fodor's reasons, and the uninterrupted answer uses first-person statements of his skeptical position.

response.rationale: This constructive move introduces the divine-psychology objection and therefore has no earlier opposing move to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly states a central objection and identifies the disputed inferential requirement.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objection is recoverable and its key terms are stable, though the phrase many philosophical arguments leaves its exact scope somewhat open.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker presents a broad concern rather than a conclusive refutation and expressly treats the relevant assumptions as uncertain.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from dependence on uncertain divine motives to reduced argumentative force is coherent, with the breadth of application left implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move identifies a real warrant problem but the excerpt supplies no representative survey showing how extensively the targeted arguments depend on it.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central philosophical-warrant bridge by challenging the predictive assumptions used in theistic arguments.

representationalCharity.rationale: The passage states a general methodological objection without developing a competing interpretation that requires a charity test.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly says many philosophical arguments require inference or knowledge about God's desires, motivations, or reasons for acting.

moves.speaker: Miles K. Donahue
moves.proposition: A perfectly good God's creative motivations can be grounded in moral value, so the goods enabled by conscious life make a life-permitting universe reasonably expected under theism.
moves.attributionBasis: Donahue identifies himself as the author of a paper on divine psychology and presents its proposed moral-value inference before requesting a response.

components.text: Whether divine creative motivation can be grounded without merely speculating about God's desires.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the decisive concern by proposing moral value as a principled basis for predicting what a perfectly good God would create.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly supplies the kind of motivation-grounding principle demanded, though its defense of that principle remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition and comparison are clear, but the ceteris-paribus limits on moving from greater moral value to greater creative likelihood remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Moral value plausibly supplies a motive, but the excerpt moves somewhat quickly from that motive to an expectation of fine-tuning.

charity.alternative: Divine motives may remain underdetermined even if conscious life realizes genuine moral goods.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply must show comparative likelihood, not merely identify one intelligible divine reason.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument has a coherent value-to-motivation-to-expectation structure, but the comparative bridge from goodness to likelihood is only partly defended.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The premise that fine-tuned conscious life enables moral goods is plausible, while the governing theory of perfect-goodness motivation is largely asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central philosophical-warrant bridge by answering the divine-motivation challenge at its main inferential point.

representationalCharity.rationale: The proposal fairly addresses underdetermination through a substantive moral principle, but does not fully establish comparative dominance over other goods.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that more morally valuable states are likelier for God to actualize and applies that principle to life-permitting fine-tuning.

moves.speaker: James Fodor
moves.proposition: Appealing to divine goodness does not make a universe like ours probable because the relevant theory of goodness is disputed and theism permits vastly many unlike creative possibilities.
moves.attributionBasis: Fodor begins by identifying the proposal as a familiar approach and then develops sustained first-person objections to both its divine and moral premises.

components.text: Whether moral value makes our life-permitting type of universe comparatively probable under theism.

response.rationale: The reply directly disputes the proposed comparative likelihood, invoking contested moral premises and the swamping effect of many alternative creations.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive probability inference and explains why identifying moral goods does not isolate our universe as expected.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objection is clear and maintains a stable comparison, while the speaker explicitly qualifies it as a still-developing judgment.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker claims lack of convincing comparative probability rather than impossibility and openly acknowledges ongoing exploration.

charity.alternative: Moral-value theory might privilege universes containing conscious agents and distinctive interpersonal goods.
charity.decisiveQualification: Privilege for some life does not by itself show that our universe or a relevantly similar universe receives substantial probability.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from numerous eligible valuable creations to underdetermined probability is strong, although no formal probability partition is supplied.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The rival-possibilities warrant is substantively explained, but the number, weighting, and representativeness of those possibilities remain undeveloped.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supports the positive-case undercut by attacking fine-tuning's claimed discriminatory likelihood under theism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply grants the moral-value strategy and targets its strongest remaining comparative-likelihood requirement rather than dismissing it superficially.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says proposed combinations of divine and moral views fail to render our universe fairly probable because other creative possibilities swamp it.

moves.speaker: Miles K. Donahue
moves.proposition: When the laws of nature and psychophysical laws are included as background information, the relevant comparison narrows to universes under which fine-tuning remains expected if theism is true.
moves.attributionBasis: Donahue calls the preceding objection strong, introduces his published response, and specifies the two groups of laws his analysis conditions upon.

components.text: Whether the relevant probability comparison is swamped by radically unlike divine creative possibilities.
Whether fine-tuning continues to rely on an uncontrolled inference about divine motivation.

response.rationale: The reply narrows the evidential comparison by conditioning on natural and psychophysical laws, thereby addressing both unrestricted possibilities and motive underdetermination.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It squarely contacts the swamping objection, though it does not fully justify treating the selected laws as legitimate background information.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditioning proposal is recoverable and technically stable, but the evidential independence required for lawful backgrounding is left implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The narrowed conditional may yield the stated expectation, but asserting that it is the relevant comparison outruns the defense supplied here.

charity.alternative: Conditioning on our laws may improperly remove evidence that itself requires explanation under the competing hypotheses.
charity.decisiveQualification: The background laws must be independently warranted rather than selected merely to exclude unfavorable creative possibilities.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional inference is internally understandable, but the crucial bridge authorizing the laws as background rather than evidence is missing.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move specifies the relevant law categories but offers little support for their independence or for the claimed expectation after conditioning.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central philosophical-warrant bridge by proposing a restricted fine-tuning comparison against the swamping challenge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response recognizes the broad possibility space but omits the strongest evidential-partition objection to its proposed narrowing.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt conditions on laws of nature and psychophysical laws and then claims that universes within that restricted class should be fine-tuned under theism.

moves.speaker: James Fodor
moves.proposition: The literary beauty and cultural importance of scripture do not establish divine inspiration because no defensible baseline distinguishes inspired texts from impressive human literature or rival scriptures.
moves.attributionBasis: The sustained answer follows Donahue's question and is delivered in Fodor's skeptical first-person voice.

components.text: Whether conditioning on natural and psychophysical laws legitimately answers the fine-tuning possibility-space objection.
Whether moral value grounds a comparative prediction of a life-permitting universe.

response.rationale: The move offers issue-bearing skeptical material about scripture, but it does not contact either earlier philosophical argument's decisive component.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is a relevant contribution to the overall positive-case dispute but is a nonanswer to the only legally earlier opposing moves.

precisionFindings.rationale: The baseline and discrimination demand is stated clearly, with rival scripture and impressive human literature explicitly defining its scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move makes the measured claim that beauty alone lacks discriminatory force absent criteria, rather than claiming scripture lacks beauty.

charity.alternative: Exceptional literary and cultural qualities might be probabilistic signs of inspiration even without a known corpus of inspired controls.
charity.decisiveQualification: A probabilistic sign still requires a defensible comparative baseline against human and rival religious texts.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from absent discriminatory baseline to failure of beauty as evidence is clear, while allowing the text's literary merit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Quran and human-literature comparisons concretely support the symmetry concern, though no systematic comparative textual evidence is presented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central positive-case undercut by challenging scriptural beauty as discriminating evidence for Christian inspiration.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection preserves the strongest aesthetic claim and accurately identifies the unresolved comparative-baseline requirement.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt compares similar claims for the Quran and asks for criteria or a baseline capable of distinguishing inspired from impressive texts.

moves.speaker: James Fodor
moves.proposition: Calling Christian religious experience self-authenticating does not resolve its epistemic weakness because it provides no reliable way to distinguish Christian revelation from rival religious experiences.
moves.attributionBasis: The answer directly follows Donahue's presentation of Craig's position and consistently expresses Fodor's skeptical epistemology.

components.text: Whether the proposed evidential background legitimately narrows the fine-tuning comparison.
Whether moral goodness supplies a sufficiently discriminating divine creative motive.

response.rationale: The religious-experience discrimination objection materially bears on the cumulative positive case but answers neither legally earlier philosophical move.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is a focused argument in a new issue area and therefore remains a relevant nonanswer to the available earlier targets.

precisionFindings.rationale: The demand for reliable discrimination is clear, and the argument consistently distinguishes private felt certainty from public epistemic reliability.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move claims an unresolved reliability problem rather than asserting that all religious experience is false or epistemically worthless.

charity.alternative: A self-authenticating experience could confer first-person warrant even if its quality cannot be communicated to outsiders.
charity.decisiveQualification: First-person certainty does not itself supply a reliable method for distinguishing incompatible religious experiences.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inability to discriminate incompatible experiences coherently undercuts self-authentication as a general reliability rule, with private warrant left possible.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual symmetry is well explained, but the excerpt supplies no representative detail about the actual range and structure of rival experiences.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supports the positive-case undercut by challenging religious experience's ability to discriminate Christianity from rival revelations.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes the proposed first-person character and targets the residual discrimination problem without reducing the view to mere testimony.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks how incompatible experiences can reliably be distinguished when only those who undergo each experience can supposedly recognize its authenticity.

moves.speaker: Miles K. Donahue
moves.proposition: Belief in God may be properly basic when grounded in coherent and undefeated direct experience of divine reality, analogously to ordinary warranted trust in the external world.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly describes his own enduring experience of God while presenting Plantinga-style reformed epistemology.

components.text: Whether direct religious experience can provide warrant despite the absence of an externally demonstrable discrimination procedure.
Whether Christian evidence has a comparative baseline against rival texts and traditions.

response.rationale: The analogy to external-world belief contacts the private-warrant issue, but it does not answer the separate comparative baseline challenge concerning scripture.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive experiential-warrant component but leaves the rival-experience discrimination condition substantially unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: Proper basicality and direct experience are used consistently, though coherence and absence of defeaters are more implicit than demonstrated in the excerpt.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker claims that belief may be justified and explicitly avoids presenting reformed epistemology as obviously decisive or incontestable.

charity.alternative: Rival religious experiences may be equally direct and properly basic for those who undergo them.
charity.decisiveQualification: Initial warrant can exist while later awareness of incompatible experiences supplies a defeater requiring discrimination.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The external-world analogy gives a coherent route to noninferential warrant, but relevant disanalogies and defeater conditions remain materially compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Personal experience and philosophical analogy support possibility, while reliability, coherence, and comparative-defeater claims receive little independent support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central Christian-evidence bridge by offering an epistemic basis for warranted belief grounded in religious experience.

representationalCharity.rationale: The analogy fairly establishes possible prima facie warrant but does not adequately incorporate the strongest disagreement-based defeater.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes Plantinga-style proper basicality and analogizes direct experience of God to ordinary warranted belief in the external world.

moves.speaker: James Fodor
moves.proposition: A temporary reburial, bereavement experiences, memory-shaping biases, and socialization can jointly explain sincere early Christian resurrection belief without a literal bodily resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: Fodor identifies the account as his RHBS model and systematically explains each naturalistic component in the first person.

components.text: Whether direct divine experience can confer properly basic warrant despite rival religious experience.

response.rationale: The naturalistic resurrection account bears on Christian evidence generally but does not address the earlier experiential-warrant inference or its defeater condition.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It supplies substantial contrary evidence in a different issue area, making it a relevant nonanswer to the available target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The RHBS account and its naturalistic components are identifiable, and the move presents them as a possible joint explanation rather than a certainty.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The account is offered as a way the belief could emerge and is explicitly characterized as drawing on existing psychological and sociological ideas.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The proposed multi-stage sequence is coherent and explanatory in outline, though dependencies among reburial, experiences, memory, and socialization are compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The speaker identifies relevant disciplinary mechanisms and historical case-study reasoning, but representative findings and their fit to this case are not documented here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary alternative-explanations bridge by supplying a naturalistic sequence for sincere resurrection belief.

representationalCharity.rationale: The selected passage principally constructs an alternative sequence and does not itself engage a sufficiently specified opposing interpretation for testing.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt labels the RHBS model and grounds it in psychology, sociology, and historical case study to explain sincere early resurrection belief.

moves.speaker: James Fodor
moves.proposition: Jewish expectations do not uniquely favor a resurrection inference, while collective experiences and a perceived empty tomb could produce bodily-resurrection belief under a naturalistic account.
moves.attributionBasis: The response directly addresses Donahue's Craig-style objection and restates distinctive elements of Fodor's naturalistic model.

components.text: Whether direct experience can make theistic belief properly basic in the face of epistemic competitors.

response.rationale: The move advances the resurrection alternative by explaining an empty tomb and bodily interpretation, but it does not contact experiential proper basicality.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is material to the broader Christian-evidence dispute while remaining a nonanswer to the only legally available opposing target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The naturalistic account's predicted empty tomb, appearances, and bodily interpretation are clearly identified without unstable terminology.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker argues that the same observations are available on his account, a comparative possibility claim proportionate to the excerpt's support.

charity.alternative: Jewish background plus an empty tomb and vivid appearances may favor bodily resurrection over ordinary bereavement experience.
charity.decisiveQualification: The observations favor resurrection only if the naturalistic sequence cannot independently predict both emptiness and bodily interpretation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Showing that the alternative predicts an empty tomb and bodily-seeming experiences directly addresses uniqueness, though the mechanisms remain abbreviated.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The model supplies a relevant explanatory comparison, but the historical and psychological frequencies required to assess its probability are not established.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary naturalistic-alternatives bridge by extending the account to specifically bodily resurrection belief.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response takes the bodily character seriously and attempts to reproduce it within the alternative rather than substituting a merely spiritual belief.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that Fodor's account, like Craig's, includes an empty tomb and appearances understood as bodily rather than merely spiritual.

moves.speaker: Miles K. Donahue
moves.proposition: Physical appearances of Jesus better explain both the reported phenomenological character of the appearances and the disciples' specifically bodily interpretation of their experiences.
moves.attributionBasis: Donahue explicitly frames the passage as advocacy for Craig and develops the resurrection explanation against Fodor's characterization.

components.text: Whether a naturalistic account adequately explains the physical phenomenology and specifically bodily interpretation of the appearances.
Whether the RHBS sequence explains the reported appearance evidence as well as physical resurrection.

response.rationale: The reply directly argues that hallucination-style mechanisms fail to explain the appearance phenomenology and that physical resurrection better explains both con moves.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive comparative-explanation issue explicitly, though the evidential details of the reported phenomenology are not developed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The explanatory claim is clear and stable, but the evidential status and scope of the appearance narratives are left as implicit qualifications.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Physical appearances would explain bodily interpretation, but the superiority claim exceeds the excerpt's limited defense of the narrative evidence.

charity.alternative: Naturalistic experiences plus an empty tomb and social interpretation could generate bodily belief without a physical Jesus.
charity.decisiveQualification: That account must explain the reported alive-and-present phenomenology rather than only the conclusion later drawn from it.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The resurrection-to-physical-appearance-to-bodily-belief inference is coherent, with a bounded gap in comparing all mechanisms of the rival sequence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move cites reported phenomenological and narrative features but does not establish their historical reliability or compare their likelihood systematically.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central Christian-evidence bridge by claiming superior explanation of the resurrection appearance evidence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply addresses the alternative's strongest combined form, but labels its experience mechanisms too narrowly as hallucinations.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that hallucinations do not explain the reported phenomenological character and that experiences of Jesus alive are better explained by resurrection.

moves.speaker: James Fodor
moves.proposition: Extensive apparently preventable suffering is unexpected if a perfectly good and powerful God created the world to realize morally valuable well-being.
moves.attributionBasis: Fodor begins the requested explanation of the problem of evil and develops it continuously through the delivered context boundary.

response.rationale: This constructive move introduces the evidential problem of apparently preventable suffering and has no earlier target requirement.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly links a major observed feature of the world to a comparative expectation under traditional theism.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is framed conditionally on traditional divine attributes and morally valuable creation, keeping both scope and key terms controlled.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker treats the argument's force as contingent on one's account of God and divine reasons, appropriately limiting the conclusion.

charity.alternative: A perfectly good God may permit suffering for goods, freedom, soul-making, or consequences unavailable without it.
charity.decisiveQualification: Such possibilities answer the evidence only if they make the observed extent of apparently preventable suffering reasonably expected.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparative inference from perfect goodness and power to an expectation of less preventable suffering is coherent and appropriately conditional.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Extensive suffering is a concrete evidential datum, but the excerpt does not specify representative cases or quantify comparative expectations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central world-evidence bridge by arguing that observed suffering is unexpected under the proposed Christian God.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move expressly conditions on divine reasons and targets unexpected excess rather than assuming that goodness prohibits every instance of suffering.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt frames evil as evidence against traditional theism when God creates to exemplify morally good states and possesses the relevant attributes.

moves.speaker: Miles K. Donahue
moves.proposition: Because historical consequences are deeply interconnected and compound beyond human prediction, only an omniscient mind could reliably compare the total outcomes relevant to apparently gratuitous evil.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker identifies the skeptical-theist view he finds most plausible, names its consequential-complexity rationale, develops it, and asks for a response.

components.text: Whether humans can reliably judge that apparently preventable suffering lacks consequences sufficient to justify divine permission.

response.rationale: The response contacts the key inference by arguing that compounding historical consequences prevent human observers from comparing total outcomes reliably.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly challenges the skeptical likelihood judgment and states why the observer lacks the information needed for that judgment.

precisionFindings.rationale: Consequential complexity and the resulting epistemic limitation are clearly defined, with the claim presented as plausible rather than demonstrated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker repeatedly qualifies the claim and limits it to reliable total-outcome comparison, matching the argument actually supplied.

charity.alternative: Some suffering may be so apparently pointless that its evidential force survives uncertainty about remote consequences.
charity.decisiveQualification: General complexity must bear on the particular likelihood judgment without making all observed evidence indiscriminately inscrutable.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Compounding consequences coherently limit confident total-outcome judgments, but the bridge from limited knowledge to broad likelihood inscrutability remains material.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Historical sensitivity and cumulative divergence plausibly support complexity, while the claim that only near-omniscience suffices is not independently established.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central world-evidence bridge by challenging the inference from apparent preventability to evidential improbability.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response identifies a serious epistemic limitation but does not address the strongest concern about selective or globally skeptical application.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that small changes compound into divergent histories and that only an omniscient or near-omniscient mind could compare the resulting outcomes.

moves.speaker: James Fodor
moves.proposition: Geographic religious contingency and deep Christian doctrinal disagreement are more expected under naturalism than under a God who intends to reveal beliefs and practices to humanity.
moves.attributionBasis: Following an explicit topic transition and request for the skeptical argument, the speaker gives a sustained first-person explanation of two levels of religious disagreement.

response.rationale: This constructive move introduces religious contingency and doctrinal confusion as comparative world evidence and has no response target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly states observed patterns, a theistic expectation, and the contrasting naturalistic expectation.

precisionFindings.rationale: Geographic contingency, information access, and intra-Christian disagreement form a clear and consistently scoped evidential proposition.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is comparative and uses expectation language rather than necessity, with its dependence on divine revelatory intent made explicit.

charity.alternative: God may value noncoercion, cultural development, or diverse searching enough to permit uneven revelation and disagreement.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those goods must explain the geographic pattern and deep doctrinal confusion despite the posited desire for accessible revelation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from intended universal access to an expectation of less geographic and doctrinal contingency is clear and appropriately comparative.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The historical and geographic pattern is specifically identified, though representative documentation and comparison across traditions are compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central world-evidence bridge by treating persistent religious confusion as less expected under Christianity.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument conditions its force on God's intended disclosure and leaves room for reasons while preserving the unmet predictive expectation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts naturalism with an omnipotent, benevolent God who wants universal access to religious information and notes geographic contingency in access.

moves.speaker: Miles K. Donahue
moves.proposition: Christianity may accommodate religious disagreement if its likelihood under Christianity is inscrutable given consequential complexity and Molinism, or if contrary evidence is outweighed within the cumulative case.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker says the problem has core plausibility, identifies what he considers Christianity's best response, and then states a secondary cumulative-case response.

components.text: Whether geographic and doctrinal disagreement is sufficiently predictable under Christianity to function as comparative evidence.
Whether consequential complexity restricts skeptical likelihood judgments about apparently gratuitous suffering.

response.rationale: The reply directly addresses disagreement through inscrutability and cumulative outweighing, while extending the earlier consequential-complexity defense.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive comparative-likelihood demand but principally asserts complexity and outweighing rather than demonstrating either.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two proposed responses—inscrutable likelihood and cumulative outweighing—are distinguishable and expressly presented as alternatives.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker says Christianity may accommodate the evidence and identifies these as possible responses, not as a demonstrated defeat.

charity.alternative: Geographic and doctrinal contingency remains predictable evidence even if remote consequences and counterfactual freedom are complex.
charity.decisiveQualification: Invoking complexity must explain why the negative likelihood is inaccessible without equally disabling favorable Christian likelihood judgments.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Either inscrutability or outweighing could limit the conclusion, but consequential complexity and Molinism are not connected in enough detail to establish this.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move names possible frameworks but supplies little concrete support that disagreement's likelihood is inscrutable or that contrary evidence actually outweighs it.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports central defeater control by offering two ways religious disagreement might fail to defeat the cumulative Christian case.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes the evidential form but leaves the strongest consistency challenge to selective inscrutability unanswered.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly claims religious disagreement may have inscrutable likelihood under Christianity because of consequential complexity and Molinism, with cumulative outweighing as another response.

moves.speaker: Miles K. Donahue
moves.proposition: Broad philosophical opinion is weak evidence against theism because most philosophers lack specialist knowledge of contemporary philosophy of religion, while specialist opinion is affected by selection effects.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn explicitly presents a response from the theistic perspective and uses first-person descriptions matching Donahue's stated expertise and position.

components.text: Whether geographic contingency and doctrinal disagreement are comparatively unexpected under Christianity.
Whether apparently preventable suffering is unlikely under a perfectly good and powerful God.

response.rationale: The move advances relevant material about expert disagreement, but it does not answer either earlier con move's decisive world-evidence component.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is important to defeater control and social epistemology, yet remains a relevant nonanswer to the legally available earlier targets.

precisionFindings.rationale: The general-versus-specialist distinction is clear, but relevant expertise and the magnitude of alleged selection effects are only partly delimited.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Breadth of philosophy supports caution about general polls, but the stronger dismissal and selection-effect claim need further comparative support.

charity.alternative: Broad philosophical opinion can remain evidence because adjacent specialties bear on theism and specialist populations may be positively selected.
charity.decisiveQualification: Reduced individual specialization does not make aggregate informed opinion insignificant, and selection effects require direction and magnitude evidence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between general and specialist expertise is coherent, but the inference to weak aggregate evidence and offsetting selection is incomplete.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The field's breadth is a plausible observation, while claims about knowledge deficits and selection effects are asserted without representative data.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supports defeater control by attempting to reduce the evidential force of broad and specialist expert dissent.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response notes disciplinary breadth but understates the strongest aggregate-evidence interpretation and does not substantiate specialist selection effects.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that philosophy is too expansive for general philosophers' views on philosophy of religion to carry substantial specialist evidential weight.

moves.speaker: James Fodor
moves.proposition: Persistent disagreement among informed people requires substantial moderation of confidence even when its exact degree is uncertain and relevant expertise extends beyond philosophy of religion.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker defends the previously introduced ten-percent estimate and explicitly frames it as his personal conciliatory judgment, identifying the turn as Fodor's.

components.text: Whether informed disagreement has substantial evidential force despite specialization limits and selection effects.
Whether uncertainty about disagreement permits maintaining very strong Christian confidence.

response.rationale: The reply directly argues that sufficient informed dissent exists across relevant areas to require moderation even if the exact adjustment is uncertain.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts both the expertise objection and the confidence consequence, while conceding uncertainty about the adjustment's size.

precisionFindings.rationale: The moderation claim, informed-person reference class, and uncertainty about degree are clearly distinguished and consistently maintained.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker claims confidence should move away from extremes while expressly declining to claim precision about how far it must move.

charity.alternative: Specialists may rationally retain high confidence because they possess discriminating evidence unavailable to broader philosophical opinion.
charity.decisiveQualification: Persistent dissent among knowledgeable specialists and adjacent experts still requires an account before near-certainty is rational.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from substantial informed disagreement to moderation away from extreme confidence is coherent, while the exact update properly remains open.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move cites specialist disagreement and cross-area knowledge, but the approximate survey figure and reference class are not documented in the excerpt.
